There’s no overstating the centrality of seals to Greenland.","formats":[]}],"__typename":"TextRunKV"}],"__typename":"VisualEssayCard"},{"key":"4980603.848698708","data":"{\"media\":[{\"id\":\"100000010829335\",\"credit\":\"\",\"altText\":\"\"}],\"mediaLayout\":\"halfBleed2by3\"}","text":[],"__typename":"VisualEssayCard"},{"key":"5557716.408579611","data":"{\"mediaLayout\":\"fullBleed\"}","text":[{"key":"body","content":[{"__typename":"TextInline","text":"International groups have campaigned against seal hunting for years, calling it cruel. ","formats":[]},{"__typename":"LineBreakInline","type":null},{"__typename":"LineBreakInline","type":null},{"__typename":"TextInline","text":"And some countries, including the United States, ban seal products, though others carve out exemptions for items produced by indigenous hunters.","formats":[]}],"__typename":"TextRunKV"}],"__typename":"VisualEssayCard"},{"key":"8862569.377878388","data":"{\"media\":[{\"id\":\"100000010829416\",\"credit\":\"\",\"altText\":\"\"},{\"id\":\"100000010829414\",\"credit\":\"\",\"altText\":\"\"}],\"mediaLayout\":\"diptych3by2\"}","text":[],"__typename":"VisualEssayCard"},{"key":"8439464.702412656","data":"{\"mediaLayout\":\"fullBleed\"}","text":[{"key":"body","content":[{"__typename":"TextInline","text":"In Greenland, the sealskin trade is a major enterprise, providing income for thousands of Inuit hunters.","formats":[]},{"__typename":"LineBreakInline","type":null},{"__typename":"LineBreakInline","type":null},{"__typename":"TextInline","text":"After they butcher the seals, they sell the skins. It’s then a long process to turn them into clothing.","formats":[]}],"__typename":"TextRunKV"}],"__typename":"VisualEssayCard"},{"key":"4950828.501171876","data":"{\"media\":[{\"id\":\"100000010829424\",\"credit\":\"\",\"altText\":\"\"},{\"id\":\"100000010829425\",\"credit\":\"\",\"altText\":\"\"}],\"mediaLayout\":\"diptych3by2\"}","text":[],"__typename":"VisualEssayCard"},{"key":"4628481.362813952","data":"{\"mediaLayout\":\"fullBleed\"}","text":[{"key":"body","content":[{"__typename":"TextInline","text":"First, the fat is removed with rollers. Blame communism, of course! But according to the Times columnist Jamelle Bouie, “There isn’t a communist wave waiting to take over America.“ Instead, he says, this “red scare” is just a distraction from the Republicans’ failure to do anything they promised to do.","transcript":"“Communism.” “Communism is a loser, and it always will be.” The president has spoken at several occasions about the dangers that communism poses to Americans. “It’s like a cancer, you got to cut it out. You got to cut it out fast.” And this is totally bizarre. “This is a full-blown communist revolution.” “We’re fighting communism on our own shores.” Things are not looking good for the G.O.P. in November. “These are numbers that Republicans do not want to see going into a midterm election.” One might think that you would try to do something to show that you are working on the economic issues that Americans say that they really care about. But you would be wrong. “Communism is on the ballot this November.” What they’re trying instead is a little bit of a Red Scare. “These are hard-core, godless communists.” They’re running against communism. “This is the most serious threat to our country since its existence.” The State Department recently put out a report alleging a decades-long plot by Cuba to inculcate communism on American shores. “You’ll live in squalor. There will be no food. There will be no housing. There will be no military. There will be no law and order. There will be no nothing. You’ll suffer and die. This is what happens.” In places like New York, Americans have elected democratic socialists. “When they say, ‘social democrats, we’re social democrats,’ it sounds so nice. It’s not nice. It’s a very dangerous term.” But democratic socialists aren’t communists, first of all, and second of all, their democratic socialism looks an awful lot like New Deal liberalism. Like something that’s very much part of the American political tradition. “This entire race was about the question of affordability.” It’s clear that when the administration and its allies say \"communism,\" they kind of just mean anyone to the left of Ronald Reagan. But nonetheless, it’s worth taking a little bit seriously the claim that communism is on the rise, and it’s not. It is true that more Americans have a positive view of socialism. And that has a lot to do with the profound failures of capitalism over the last 20 years. Americans who remember the financial crisis. Americans who are looking at, again, rising prices, at a labor market that’s difficult to break into if you’re young. Food insecurity. They’re looking at these things and saying, \"I don’t know if capitalism is great for us.\" So much of the Trump administration seems to be an effort to recapitulate things from the past as almost like a magic incantation that if you say them the right way, you’ll get the same effects. “Make America great again.” And I have a feeling that Trump who came up under the tutelage of Roy Cohn. thinks that if you just do a Red Scare, you’ll get voters behind you. “In this committee, activities may well determine whether this nation will live or die.” But the Red Scare was a particular response to a particular era, and even then, it wasn’t that politically successful for the people who initiated it. “Have you no sense of decency, sir?” And here, it’s not going to do much good for Trump. The fact of the matter is, is that, a, there isn’t some communist wave coming to take over America, and b, the president’s political woes, like the Republican Party’s, has everything to do with the failure of this administration to do anything it promised to do, and instead to focus on its narrow preoccupations. To bring so much joy to families, for them especially those families that have previous generations of Knicks fans who have been just begging for a chance to be in the N.B.A. Finals, let alone winning the N.B.A. Finals after 53 years, and then last time being 27 years ago against the Spurs, too, ironically. I feel like a “Love Island” character getting back my phone after the playoffs and seeing these, these reels and these videos and these and these Instagram posts about the grandfather celebrating it with his son’s kid, and passing that kind of Knicks fandom down to the kid or the father who grew up watching the disappointment of 1999 or families and those people who have — those lost loved ones and, and going to the cemetery to celebrate the Knicks win with them. And I know how special it is because I saw people in Brooklyn cheering and they got their own N.B.A. team. So that’s kind of — that’s kind of crazy to do. But it just shows, you know, New York’s so unified with each other when you give them something to be unified for and for us to reach the mountaintop and give so many people something to cheer for and so many people to have hope for. An Israeli Strike Ended Her Dreams.","__typename":"CreativeWorkHeadline"},"__typename":"Video","id":"VmlkZW86bnl0Oi8vdmlkZW8vODI2NjAyMDctMWQwMy01NWUzLWE5NzUtNThkMDU5Y2M3ZGVm","uri":"nyt:\u002F\u002Fvideo\u002F82660207-1d03-55e3-a975-58d059cc7def","url":"https:\u002F\u002Fwww.nytimes.com\u002Fvideo\u002Fworld\u002Fmiddleeast\u002F100000011002217\u002Fgaza-palestine-israel-student-raghad-ashour.html","summary":"Since the cease-fire in October, Israeli forces have killed one child or teenager in Gaza every day on average, according to UNICEF. Raghad Ashour, an ambitious 17-year-old student, became one of them when she was hit by an airstrike as she walked home from school.","transcript":"A mother grieves the loss of her teenage daughter in an Israeli strike in Gaza. In late June, Samha Ashour asked her daughter, Raghad, to pick up bread and herbs on her way home from school. She was killed crossing a busy street. The 17-year-old was a bright and ambitious student, according to her relatives and teachers. But, like so many other young lives cut short by the violence in Gaza, a strike ended Raghad’s dreams of a better life. We obtained and verified graphic videos showing how the blast unfolded. In this security footage from a nearby internet lounge, people inside recoil from the impact of the initial strike. The owner of the space runs out and starts recording on his phone. Another video shows Raghad’s body on the ground next to a black car. As crowds rush toward where she is, a final missile falls from the sky. Roughly two minutes passed between the first strike and the last strike. The Israeli Army said it had been targeting a Hamas militant traveling in a vehicle. The army did not confirm whether it had killed its target. Local emergency services said three people had been injured in the attack. A spokesperson for Gaza’s health ministry told The Times that Raghad was the only person killed. In a statement, the Israeli military said it regretted any harm to uninvolved civilians. Samha and her daughter shared this small space in an encampment for Gaza’s displaced. Raghad was about to enter her final year of high school, and she had just been accepted into her school’s artificial intelligence program. According to UNICEF, at least one child or teenager has been killed on average every day since the cease-fire was announced nine months ago. Video and images provided by her family show a snapshot of how Raghad lived as a war raged around her. Here, she is celebrating her last birthday at a restaurant in Gaza. She also volunteered as a mentor for younger children as part of a UNICEF program called Youth Champions. Raghad’s teacher told us about her dedication to her studies. Gaza’s education system has been decimated by the war. And Raghad’s school was one of the few still functioning after more than 90 percent were destroyed or damaged, according to UNICEF. Raghad’s short life is now one of the many grim statistics in Gaza, leaving behind an exhausted family in a floundering Carter Sherman argues that millennials were already having less sex than previous generations — changing how we should think about what’s happening today.","transcript":"But is it uncool to not be able to have sex? Because I think it’s perceived as cool to choose not to have sex. Something that I do think that comes up a lot that sometimes frustrates me when we talk about Gen Z and the sex recession is millennials were also having less sex. So like, while we were having all of this discussion around, oh, they’re hooking up too much, like, the reality is that they were having less sex than previous generations. And so when we think about the causes of the sex recession, I think we have to remember this started before #MeToo. This started before the pandemic. Like, Gen Z is the inheritors of a trend that began among millennials. So whatever we’re seeing with Gen Z, how they see relationships, how they see hooking up, like, we have to be looking at both generations and thinking about things that have happened with both What we’re telling the Canadians is all we’re expecting you to do — basically, be llke the Germans or the Poles. Get you — use your defense, increase Canadian defense dollars to buy real military capability that fills joint needs because that —and that’s not just a nice-to-have that affects America. This is good and I’m all for that. But you’re doing that while the president is, appearing on TV or in a video still or wherever else it is with a map showing the U.S. Stars and Stripes covering North America. Which is different. That’s different. That’s a different policy ask from more defense. Well, I don’t think it’s a different — I mean, I don’t think what we’re doing is different than what he’s doing. He’s — What is he doing? I wouldn’t presume to characterize what the president is doing. Well, then how do it’s not different from what you’re doing? I wouldn’t —it’s certainly not incompatible. I mean, I think the president, as I understand it, is communicating that the United States needs to be secure and have our interests respected in the hemisphere, and he communicates it in that way. So you interpret, you interpret the image of the Stars and Stripes flying up past Hudson Bay as just the Monroe Doctrine. Well, I think the Stars and — Stars and Stripes should be flying high above anywhere. So it’s great. We’re proud of it. It’s 250 years and flying. Flying anywhere is a statement of sovereignty or just as a statement of awesomeness? Well, what do you mean? But what do you — what do you mean? You think the Stars and Stripes should be flying — Well, I just think the president has been saying when he’s talked about it, he says that the Canadians have an insanely favorable trading arrangement and that they’re relying almost right on the American economy and that needs to be recalibrated. And that’s all you think he’s saying? I know you don’t presume to to speak for him. I think it speaks for itself.
